nodes.question: How many species of fish, prawns, and crabs are found in mangrove ecosystems?
nodes.answer: There are nearly 3000 different species of fish, prawns, and crabs in mangrove ecosystems.
nodes.paragraph: Vol. :(123456789)Environmental Science and Pollution Research https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-25-36203-y TREND EDITORIAL Coastal guardian: mangroves in Pakistan at risk from microplastic threats jeopardizing their crucial role in global CO2 dynamics Tariq Mehmood1 David Janke1 Gajendra Kumar Gaurav2 Muhammad Fahad Sardar3 Received: 16 December 2024 / Accepted: 26 February 2025 The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2025 Guardians of the coast: the critical role of mangroves on the global level The mangrove ecosystem is a unique coastal ecosystem found at the dynamic interface between the ocean and the land (Lin et al. 2024). It plays a vital role in preserving the natural ecological balance and is important to tropical and subtropical shorelines (Uddin et al. 2022). Mangroves help protect coastlines, support fishing industries, maintain bio- diversity, regulate local climates, purify the environment, promote eco-tourism, and maintain balance in coastal areas. Their work is vital to supporting the livelihoods of over 120 million individuals globally (Primavera et al. 2019). There are nearly 3000 different species of fish, prawns, and crabs (Qayyum and Rehman 2022), as well as 120 species of fungi in their surroundings (Sandilyan and Kathiresan 2012).

nodes.question: What are some factors contributing to the homogenization in the tropics mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: (1) Smaller distributional ranges than the global average, (2) a higher degree of ecological specialization, and (3) the temperate zones have already experienced large-scale homogenization.
nodes.paragraph: A further 1 2% of species could be considered non-native invasive winners. Therefore, there is an overall effect of replacing many losing species with a few winning species. This leads to assemblage homogeniza- tion of genetic and functional levels at both local and global scales (McKinney and Lockwood 1999; Olden et al. 2004; Newbold et al. 2018). Global meta-analyses indicate that homogenization is occurring globally and across taxonomic groups (McKin - ney and Lockwood 1999; Newbold et al. 2018). However, the process is currently more pronounced in the tropics (Newbold et al. 2018). This is thought to be due to: (1) dis- tributional ranges that are smaller than the global average; (2) a higher degree of ecological specialization; and (3) that temperate zones have already experienced the large-scale homogenization that the tropics are currently experiencing (Newbold et al. 2018). nodes.answer: System variability and system complexity further exacerbate the data needs for understanding ecosystems.

Those data needs are further exacerbated by system variability and system complexity (Schmeller et al. 2018). For a better understanding of the state and trends of ecosystems, independent if we want to look at ecological integrity or ecosystem health, a common measurement approach is urgently needed. As drinking water is a particularly pre- cious natural resource, we here focus on aquatic ecosystems. Water is a key element and an important resource for all living organisms, as it supplies adequate and rich environments for wildlife (Karr 2011). A plethora of parameters can be analyzed in water that allows the assessment of the status of the aquatic ecosystem by look - ing at species abundance, chemical composition, and water body condition (Burkhard et al. 2008). As ecosystems are spatially heterogeneous and vary over time, indicators or indi- ces of ecosystem health need to take this variability into account.
